What is really infuriating is the right wing pundits who are blaming the woman. Someone needed to say no, and Mr. French points that out in detail.

comments.name: Madoc
comments.body:
Nicely written Mr. French. 

But when passing judgment on ALL of these boys, I think you avoid some important points. 

First, you call them all men. They are not adult men, they are boys. Yet you call Jane doe a girl. Why? Do you believe Jane Doe is young and naive and these boys are really adult  men— they should know better ? 

Second, you indict the entire group of boys in one fraternity as lacking moral character. I think that is unfair and an example associative guilt that is plaguing so many societies today. Maybe many did not even see the snap chat or didn’t believe it etc… 

Third, you say all these boys are depraved, lacking a norm of high moral courage to stop things. Yet, you omit acknowledging the many complex societal issues at play, particularly for young people. Who is responsible for that? These boys? Society? Parents? 

It’s easy to want to paint with such broad a brush for a nice opinion piece. But I think you lack the granularity this incident deserves.

Real care for women would entail seeing them as humans equal in all ways to white men.

comments.name: Kelly Grace Smith
comments.body:
This isn't just about what porn teaches our young men about sex, it is about what our young men are taught about women.

(By the way, porn "teaches" all men, young and old.)

For a moment, iImagine a young man in that room being sodomized and raped by a group of frat boys...

Can't really imagine that? There is a reason for that and it has everything to do with how we as a society view...the value of women.

And yet, this is the year 2026. 

There is a deeper question...a question ringing out loudly all across our society, from Cornell and Tennessee, to the "detention" prisons where the human beings who used to tend to our farms and our factories, our restaurants and our backyards, are incarcerated in wholly cruel and inhumane conditions...the vast majority of them with no criminal record.

What about...our humanity? Our shared humanity?

What about the humanity, not only of the woman victim at the Cornell fraternity house, but of all those men who engaged in those acts and all the men who saw the communications that night and subsequent to that night?  

At the most profound level - should we ever choose to get real about this, should we ever stop the incessant intellectualizing about it - one thing is unalterably true...

"Without our humanity - our shared humanity - we will possess nothing of value."

comments.name: Sumner Brooks

I'm all in favor of personal responsibility, and I understand why Mr. French doesn't want to adjudicate legal responsibility here, but we are living in a time of supreme unaccountability for those at the top (like the frat brothers at Chi Phi), and until that changes, personal responsibility isn't going to prevent these abhorrent events.

As a society, we seem unable to hold accountable white men who victimize women and people of color. William Calley, who led his men to slaughter hundreds at My Lai, was convicted at court martial and sentenced to life imprisonment. The vast majority of Americans, however, were furious at the verdict, which was subsequently reduced to 20 years, then 10. He served a total of three years under house arrest.

We currently have a Secretary of War in Pete Hegseth, who revels in committing serial mass murder on fishermen off the coast of South America, and where is the outrage?

A USA Today investigation found hundreds of liens, judgments, and at least 60 lawsuits from contractors, painters, and plumbers who said they weren't paid. At the Taj Mahal, 253 subcontractors were reportedly shorted $69.5 million, and some waited three years and got about 30 cents on the dollar. One cabinet maker was never paid an $83,600 bill, and a $30,000 painting bill at Doral was denied. His casino companies filed Chapter 11 four times (1991, 1992, 2004, 2009), and bondholders and shareholders lost more than $1.5 billion.  So while Senator Roger Marshall may have not paid a small bakery bill, he has been part of two major economic wins for our nation: First economic growth is finally slowing, falling short of the dangerous 3% target. Second, the deficit continues to rise, reaching $3.1 trillion by 2036, or 120% of gross domestic product. I wish this piece had focused a bit on what to do with disposed things. 
Some people have trouble getting rid of unneeded things that are not recyclable, donatable or saleable because they hate to think of the stuff rotting in a dump for hundreds or thousands of years.

comments.name: Richard
comments.body:
Perceptions about objects vary among different people.  Some people are very sentimental about old stuff, while others toss them without a second thought.  I've seen many examples of both.

Decluttering can be both emotionally difficult--to let go of old memories and connections to now-gone loved ones.  But also physically difficult dealing with heavy old books and papers and dusty, even mildewed old stuff.  Some communities have restrictions on how much or what kinds of trash can be placed out for collection, making disposal harder.

As the baby boomers age and face downsizing, this will be an issue.  Some folks will be reluctant to part with old objects and will need gentle encouragement.

comments.name: Cailín
comments.body: Excess stuff makes me anxious. For me, Hell would not be represented by flames and demons wielding pitchforks, but rather endless shelves lined with knickknacks. I spent many hours clearing out my parents' home when my widowed mother moved to assisted living. She was a tidy hoarder, with a neat home where every cupboard and closet was full to the door. I didn't want to leave my kids the same experience and began decluttering and "Swedish Death Cleaning" as a hobby when I retired during the pandemic. I find it restful and affirming. Yes, some objects are imbued with meaning, but most are not. You are not your stuff.

comments.name: Jane
comments.body: Two years ago my husband and I sold the family home and moved downtown to a smaller condo.  We loved the house, but we love the condo even more.  We got rid of half of our stuff - unneeded furniture to our kids, nephews, nieces and Community Warehouse.   Other things to Goodwill and friends who wanted specific things.  The hardest things were my books.  I had build an entire wall of gorgeous and not so gorgeous well-loved books, many of which had crossed the country with me several times in 50 years -- "English Romantic Writers" from college with notes on Shelley, Keats and Byron in the margins.  My books on Catherine de Medici, who I had researched extensively.  Could I really get rid of them?  Should I?  Would I?  Reader, I did.  I kept enough meaningful ones for the shelves we now have - ones like the Golden Treasury of Myths and Legends that my parents gave me at age 9.  Travel books that would still be useful, along with French and Italian language books. Every beautiful art book stayed, as did books on opera and music.  Everything else went - crumbly paperback Faulkners and Edith Whartons (notes in the margins, pages almost orange from age).  I regret a few - a complete set of Dickens, some cookbooks that contained memories of great dinners past, but other than that, it is good.  I like to think my books found a happy home where someone new can experience the joy they brought to me.

comments.name: virginia
comments.body: While there's much to be said for the longing to hold on, I discovered with my daughter that the inability to declutter may be a more distinct neurological inability that actually has to do with mathematical thinking as well as some other major types of thinking: the inability to sort and categorize. Once this basic mental operation has been made, decisions about keeping or letting go are much easier to make. But without this ability, decluttering is impossible, because each item presents the entire the challenge to the person attempting to declutter.

comments.name: Alex A
comments.body:
Until charging times are short and the charging infrastructure robust, EV's are not for everyone, or for that matter not for most of us.

ER-EV's are a viable transition technology.  You can charge them at home overnight with a standard AC outlet or an inexpenisve level 2 outlet; this will be fine or errands or commuting.  When you travel just gas'em up.

PHEV's also offer this versatility, but they have less electric range and more mechanical complexity.

It's a real shame there are no ER-EV's available  in the US today.  GM pioneering this technology with the Volt, but discontinued the Volt in 2019.  If an updated version were sold today, it would likely sell well.  GM has fine engineering, but the marketing folks that control vehicle production roadmaps seem awfully nearsighted.

Finally, the nation needs standards for bidirectional charging, so that interested car owners can use their vehicles to provide power to their  homes during an outage, or perhaps help support the grid itself when regional power demand is high.

comments.name: Ed
comments.body:
As reported today in NYT, most elected officials are receiving threats from constituents. Very serious threats over the past two years. Why? A number of reasons, for sure. But a big one happens to sit at the top of our executive branch. 

Let’s take Marjorie Taylor Greene, former Republican House member from Georgia, for example. She has received threats galore. 

Voices that sounded like demons, saying they wanted to dig my brains out of my head with a screwdriver, or other calls where they said they wanted to smash my head open on a curb.

Her breaking point came after the president called her a “traitor.” Of the torrent of threats that followed, one stood out. It was aimed at her son.

“That’s the one that bothers me on a visceral level,” she said.

Ms. Greene reached out to Mr. Trump, hoping for compassion from a president she had stood by for years.

Trump’s five word response: “Your fault, you deserve it.”

Republican voters: is this really what you want in our political leadership? Think about who you are, and what kind of world you want to leave your sons and daughters. Then vote for who you really think will get our nation there.

comments.name: Craig
comments.body:
This is what happens when civil discourse collapses.  When many politicians play to the worst elements of human emotion.  When issue-based polarization dominates our culture.  When media lies knowingly and deliberately to increase their own influence.

This has nothing to do with guns.  New laws there won't address the problem.  The problem is hate.  Our little (and sometimes not so little) echo chambers reflect and amplify it.  Hate engenders fear.  Fear leads us to withdraw into our chambers, and creates a vicious cycle of amplification.  At some point, some people will break.

First things first.  Free speech should not include hate speech.  We have to move past hate speech before we can have meaningful dialogue.  Our political messaging, especially by the PACs who are accountable to no one, has to be reined in.

But...this won't happen.  Free speech is a cornerstone, but it's also a major part of the problem.  Reining in the abuses of speech has consistently failed.

But it was often thankless work and it wasn’t long before I realized the people we needed most were becoming least willing to raise their hand. Shame on those who market the indexed annuity product without positively confirming with the prospective buyer that they understand the dollars and cents that they will lose when the cap is adjusted downward.

2) No wonder Delaware Life got into trouble.  Turning $100,000 into $2.7 million in just 21 years is based on an outrageous assumption.  The annualized growth would have to be 16.99 percent for EACH of the 21 years to realize a compounded growth resulting in $2.7 million.  Is there a sucker born every minute?

MFA is now considered to be obsolete, the WSJ info is not very current. These comments from an AI tool on what works best today where hackers have AI tools to get past passwords are very interesting:

  1. Passkeys & FIDO2/WebAuthn: The most practical upgrade to consumer and enterprise security is the widespread adoption of passkeys. Based on public-key cryptography, passkeys bind the login attempt to the specific, verified domain (RP ID) in the browser. Because there is no shared secret (like a password) stored on a server and no code sent via SMS, an AI agent cannot guess it, brute-force it, or trick a user into handing it over.2. Hardware Security Keys: For critical infrastructure and developer accounts (like GitHub or AWS where API keys often leak), physical security keys (e.g., YubiKeys) enforcing FIDO2 offer the strongest defense against unauthorized logins.3. Zero-Trust Identity & Short-Lived Tokens: For automated systems and APIs, static credentials stored in code repositories must be eliminated entirely. Moving to short-lived, environment-bound tokens ensures that even if an AI agent discovers a credential, it becomes useless almost immediately

Bill

comments.name: Ed Williams
comments.body:
If you have your own wifi access point (the wifi transmitter, your cable router, etc) you should do at least 2 things: turn on encryption, and turn off the SSID announcement.

The first means that any user of your wifi needs the password for your wifi, they can't just connect.  Without this anyone can connect.  This is often but not always on by default, so check it.

The second means that your wifi is not spending all day every day broadcasting "I'm here and my name is..." so everybody in range can see it.  Devices can still use it, but they have to know the name of your wifi before they can connect.

If you need more security, because you have valuable stuff attached to you network, there are more complex actions you can take to control who can use it and what they do.  

If you use someone else's wifi you need to think about how much you trust them, and with what you trust them.  Probably take a few extra steps, like at minimum be sure the connect to the website uses HTTPS not just HTTP, or use a VPN.  Just realize that nothing is perfect, just better or worse.

comments.name: W.
comments.body:
What a nice story, I didn’t think Hungarian folks reality would be on my radar today.
Shows the disparity between folks isn’t just with the US, a lot of politicians have their foot on that old gas. I do wonder though, if a rooster brings this much passion..What would a friendly dog or cat do for this community? I’d guess a lot.

comments.name: MustWithHoldThisTime
comments.body: A poignant parable of community lost, gained, and fragmented. Bekescsaba, Hungary's town square represents and invites community by design, but struggles against government policy that crush community spirit.

comments.name: Erika
comments.body: The images of the plastic wrapped live chickens is just horrible. Maybe when humans treat animals with compassion and love, this world will be a better place.

comments.name: Wolfy Amadeus Mole
comments.body: What an amazing story, how a brave rooster became an integral part of a community. He was a true local hero. This movie was like a fairy-tale come to life. Bravo Sanyi and R.I.P.

articles.title: The Rooster That Brought a Hungarian Town Together
articles.summary: A Hungarian town, an escaped rooster and the universal longing for freedom.

comments.name: V
comments.body: I read this piece and I am left wondering what I learned or even understood. It is possible that I don’t have the deep thoughtfulness that nytimes expects of its readers but I have this feeling that I am sometimes reading articles that exist for the sake of existing. In fact, sometimes I find the regular news sections to be so unecessarily long that I think there must be some incentive that stopped working as a performance metric long ago. Clearly, printed paper kept a lid on some of these things but in the digital era it’s like swimming in text that is searching for meaning instead of the other way around.

comments.name: INCLUDE ME OUT
comments.body:
Did the acquisition of great wealth create the arrogance demonstrated by the likes of Zuckerberg, Musk and others?

Or did a pre-existent arrogance within them help to enable their financial success?

I tend to believe the former, with perhaps just a tad bit of the latter.

comments.name: Cannoneers74
comments.body:
Zuckerberg seems an awkward fellow who has never fit in socially. He finds himself in a place where he will, chameleon-like, morph into whatever persona is necessary to further his business. He can be liberal or conservative depending on the prevailing political winds. If he needs to be more cage-fighter masculine or Joe Rogan political, he will take lessons and become so. 

He seems a lump of clay that will attempt to take on a personality that is presently convenient, but still seems awkward doing so. 

I think he must be a lonely character.

comments.name: Serena Kratz
comments.body: A Man who has no moral compass. He thinks nothing of what impact his company has on people, countries and the world.  Huegens book " Carless People" should be required reading in all business schools as a moral warning of what not to be and do.  He was always an entitled person before he created Meta and now he is just one of many technocrats who think that they and they alone know anything worth knowing.  .

comments.name: abraham quisling
comments.body: you’d think they would have updated zuck’s software by now to make him more human-like.

comments.name: DM
comments.body:
“the corporate world is pretty culturally neutered” and calling for “masculine energy” and “a culture that celebrates the aggression a bit more.”

This is a man with no experience of the world before his living memory. I mean, the 80s, Gordon Gecko and "greed is good". How could anyone miss previous overly-macho decades, if there is ever not one?

comments.name: V
comments.body:
I mean people are generally complex and hard to pigeonhole as one type of person. Like the line from Walt Whitman “do i contradict myself? Very well I contradict myself, I am large, I contain multitudes”
He could very well be all of those characters (not the Eisenberg one) or all of it’s an act.

comments.name: Victoria
comments.body: Thought strong caught the essence but he seemed a bit overly stiff. But then he knows more than I do. But he certainly made him unlikable. Very hard to watch.

articles.title: Three Mark Zuckerbergs, Three Surprisingly Different Men
articles.summary: Jeremy Strong in “The Social Reckoning,” Jesse Eisenberg in “The Social Network” and the real Meta executive are all playing parts. But only one has changed his approach.

comments.name: Harriet Griffey
comments.body: I was the editor who worked with Hite on the republication of various titles — including The Hite Report on Men — in the 1990s & to whom she said she kissed (not licked) her handsome young husband’s teeth, as teeth survive after death.

comments.name: hd
comments.body: loved this but would have appreciated Alexandra Jacobs sparing a sentence (at least) on what was in the "Hite Report"

comments.name: formerlyspinet
comments.body:
"like Sherry without the y?" um
...why not simply like SHARE or better yet CHER?

comments.name: teach
comments.body: I'm so thankful that I had women like Steinhem and Hite as models in my early adulthood.  Gosh, they still seem so much more real and "out" as human beings than most people in the limelight now.

comments.name: Theresa
comments.body: Our Bodies Ourselves, The Hite Report, The Sensous Woman by J, Our Secret Garden,  provided me as a college junior an education in my body and what sex could be but at that point certainly was lacking in my actual experience. I thank all the authors. My poor mother did her best but was so embarrassed she never got past “ it’s a beautiful thing that can happen between a husband and wife”.

comments.name: Hortense
comments.body: As always, Alexandra Jacobs delivers a witty and interesting review, in this case of a book that seems like it's probably not as fascinating as it should have been, given the subject. Great review, anyway, and great subject.

comments.name: Elinct
comments.body:
I wish you had named the documentary . It is" The Disappearance of Shere Hite". It is fascinating and wonderful portrait of a ground braking woman with fantastic archival footage. Shocking how she was dismissed and condescended to.
I very highly recommend it!

comments.name: Fg
comments.body: "A typewriter so smart she doesn't have to be" is a line that brings back the pain of being an early female boomer who saw little opportunity to find a fulfilling career or the respect that we all deserved and were instead relegated to using typewriters that were  "smarter "than us and taking a back seat in our careers to men who were "more qualified" than we were.  Thank goodness for fighters like Shere Hite who helped break these barriers to equality giving the rest of us a little gumption to fight for ourselves, even if we often won a few battles but lost the war as I did in taking legal action for an equal salary and being punished by losing my job and my career and this still happened in the late nineties.  Sad.

articles.title: 50 Years Later, a Hit Book on Women’s Sexuality Deserves Some Love
articles.summary: Its author became a pop culture celebrity, and sometimes punchline, but “The Hite Report” helped make way for frank discussions about pleasure.

comments.name: L
comments.body: Neither Dave Barnett nor Birding Bob are ethical birders that follow guidelines, they call birds on and harasses birds like owls. Would love to see responsible birders quoted rather than those who have built followings by harming birds.

comments.name: Don
comments.body: One great threat to barn owls are great horned owls, which displaced our resident family. Barn owls screech, great horned owls hoot. Hoping for lots of screeching and no hooting on the upper west side.

comments.name: J. Daniel Von Peartree
comments.body: The story is great and the photos are gorgeous.

comments.name: Dan Hewson
comments.body: This is the best bird story in the big city I've yet seen. The fact that it's a large family makes it truly unique. I hope it's just a vacation of sorts for the Owls, as true wilderness is a better option for a healthy life for these beautiful birds.

comments.name: Christopher Maag
comments.body: I love stories of awe and delight. When I was assigned to write about New York's latest celebrity owl -- who isn't just one bird but an entire family, including adolescents learning to fly -- my only thought was YES.

comments.name: A pea in the ocean
comments.body: This is the best.  Despite looking hard to see a Barn Owl in the United States, I have never been successful.  That is, with the exception of a dead one in southeast Arizona.  Now, a long over due visit to NYC is calling my name.  I can hear the owls screeches from here.

comments.name: N. Smith
comments.body: No doubt many world-weary New Yorkers will kindly think of 'Flaco', the Eurasian eagle-owl who captured our attention -- and ultimately, our hearts....and I will be one of them.

articles.title: New York’s Latest Famous Family Is a Hoot. Yes, They’re Owls.
articles.summary: The city’s latest feathered extraordinaires are captivating the Upper West Side with their screeches.
